"The coronavirus outbreak has harmed communities and disrupted economic activity in many countries, including the United States."

Literature-consistent assessment: The statement reflects a negative common shock that depresses output and heightens deflation risk. Credit and balance-sheet channels can amplify downturns when financial conditions tighten and firm net worth deteriorates (Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994; Gertler and Gilchrist, 1994; Oliner and Rudebusch, 1996a). Declines in market-based inflation compensation imply weaker expected inflation, which raises real interest rates and restrains spending in standard macro models linking expectations to aggregate demand. While the FOMC’s countercyclical easing and asset purchases are consistent with the literature on stabilization policy and can cushion the shock, the immediate disruption and amplification mechanisms justify a moderately negative tone.
